title: Vision-Based Gesture Control for Industrial Automation: A Review of MediaPipe Hand Landmark Recognition and Human–Robot Interaction

authors.name: Prof. Markus J. Weber
authors.affiliation: Department of Mechanical Engineering, Technical University of Munich

abstract: Vision-based gesture control provides an attractive hands-free interface for human–robot interaction (HRI) in industrial automation, but practical deployment remains constrained by sensing variability, latency, and safety integration. This paper reviews the use of MediaPipe hand landmark recognition as a practical engine for industrial gesture control and surveys algorithmic, hardware, and systems-level considerations needed for factory-floor use. We analyze landmark normalization, temporal filtering, feature extraction, classifier design, and PLC integration, and report a representative experimental evaluation from the Robotics Lab at the Technical University of Munich showing a prototype achieving 95.4% accuracy and 12.3 ms median inference latency on an Intel i7 industrial PC communicating via Profinet to a Siemens S7-1500. The review highlights robustness tradeoffs under occlusion and illumination changes and provides reproducible parameter sets, wiring recommendations, and safety integration patterns useful for engineers and researchers seeking production-ready gesture control. Practical limitations and future research directions are discussed.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: Gesture interfaces promise natural, low-effort command channels for industrial workers operating in constrained or safety-critical environments. In modern factories, the ability to issue start/stop, speed-change, or acknowledge commands without touching a shared control panel can reduce contamination, speed workflows, and complement traditional HMIs. The confluence of high-quality commodity cameras, deterministic fieldbus networks, and mature perception pipelines such as MediaPipe [1] makes deployment of vision-based gesture control technically feasible on production lines. However, reliability under industrial lighting, consistent landmark localization, and safe interfacing to PLCs remain open engineering tasks that must be addressed before widespread adoption.

Prior work has explored gesture recognition in lab and consumer settings [2][3] and has investigated industrial HRI using wearable sensors [4] and depth cameras [5]. MediaPipe’s hand landmark approach [1], which outputs $N=21$ normalized 2D/3D points per detected hand, reduces the need for costly depth sensors and provides a compact intermediate representation that is attractive for embedded and edge inference. Yet many published evaluations are limited to consumer datasets or report latency and accuracy without examining PLC integration, network determinism, or long-term reliability on factory floors [6][7]. These practical limitations have slowed industrial uptake.

This review aims to synthesize the technical ingredients required to move from research prototypes to production-grade gesture control systems. We focus on MediaPipe-based pipelines because of their lightweight landmark output, documented models, and widespread adoption in robotics research. The research gap we address is the lack of a single, technically detailed resource that combines algorithmic descriptions, wiring and integration patterns for common industrial hardware (e.g., Basler cameras, Siemens S7 PLCs, ABB manipulators), performance metrics under industrial constraints, and honest discussion of deployment risks.

We present a structured review and a representative prototype evaluation developed at the Robotics Lab, Department of Mechanical Engineering, Technical University of Munich. Contributions of this paper are:
1) A systems-level taxonomy that connects camera selection, landmark normalization, temporal filtering, classification, and PLC integration.
2) Concrete algorithmic patterns and equations for landmark normalization, temporal smoothing, feature extraction, and evaluation metrics, with recommended parameter values validated in our testbed.
3) Wiring, network, and safety recommendations for integrating the perception pipeline with Profinet and Siemens S7-1500 PLCs, including measured latencies and failure modes.
4) An experimental study reporting $95.4\%$ accuracy and 12.3 ms median inference latency on a representative industrial rig, plus ablation results against conventional classifiers.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II surveys related literature on gesture recognition, MediaPipe, and industrial interfaces. Section III describes the system architecture and methodology used for normalization, filtering, and classification, including equations and wiring recommendations. Section IV presents experimental setup, quantitative results, comparisons to prior methods, and endurance tests. Section V summarizes findings, candidly lists limitations, and outlines concrete directions for future work.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: This section summarizes prior literature across three threads: gesture recognition methods with visual sensors, MediaPipe and hand landmark research, and industrial HRI and PLC integration. The subsections below give detailed critiques and deployment-focused distinctions.

content.text: Early approaches to vision-based gesture recognition relied on hand-crafted features such as skin color segmentation, optical flow, and hand silhouette shape descriptors [2][8]. These methods performed adequately in constrained lighting but were brittle under variability common in industrial environments, such as fluorescent flicker and specular reflections on metallic surfaces. The shift to deep learning introduced convolutional networks trained on large datasets (e.g., EgoGesture, Chalearn) and improved robustness to background clutter [3][9]. A practical limitation of end-to-end CNN approaches in industry is their input size and inference cost: many CNNs expect full-frame images of size $224\times224$ or larger and require GPUs for low-latency operation, which complicates integration into deterministic PLC loops [10].

Hybrid approaches decouple detection and classification by extracting keypoints or landmarks and feeding compact features to lighter-weight classifiers such as SVMs or shallow MLPs [11][12]. This reduces inference load and allows deployment on industrial PCs with commodity CPUs. However, prior studies often omit wiring, grounding, and fieldbus considerations, which are essential for IEC 61508 compliance in safety-related applications [13]. Another issue is temporal stability: many methods classify frames independently, producing jitter in downstream actuators unless explicit smoothing or state machines are added [14].

Recent publications explored multimodal fusion (RGB+IMU) for gestures to increase robustness [4][15]. While fusion typically improves accuracy, wearable IMUs impose worker acceptance and maintenance challenges on factory floors, and they add procurement and sanitation overhead. From a deployment perspective, camera-only systems that provide $N=21$ landmarks (see Section III) are attractive because they reduce operator instrumentation while maintaining good discriminative power when combined with temporal filters.

content.text: Fig. 1 (above) contextualizes the evolution from early silhouette methods to lightweight landmark approaches. The figure highlights why a MediaPipe-based pipeline often provides the best compromise for industrial HRI: compact feature vectors, moderate CPU cost, and clear upgrade paths to state estimation and multi-sensor fusion [1][11].

MediaPipe Hands [1] introduced a two-stage pipeline: a palm detection stage followed by a landmark regression stage that returns $N=21$ 2D coordinates and optionally relative depth per landmark. Several groups have validated MediaPipe performance on consumer datasets and in robotic teleoperation [16][17]. A technical advantage is the explicit landmark representation, which decouples perception from task-specific classifiers. This decoupling simplifies feature engineering (angles, normalized distances) and enables rapid retraining of classification layers with limited labeled data.

A key technical limitation found in prior empirical studies is sensitivity to partial occlusion and extreme viewing angles. MediaPipe’s regression is trained on mixed datasets but is not explicitly tuned for strong industrial occlusions caused by gloves, tool-holding poses, or protective screens. Several attempts to reduce this sensitivity used temporal models (LSTM, temporal convolution) or additional camera views to produce robust tracking [18][19]. These remedies improve robustness but increase system complexity and synchronization requirements, which in turn places stricter demands on the network and time-stamping mechanisms in the data pipeline.

From a systems perspective, MediaPipe’s inference grid and available ONNX exports facilitate deployment on industrial PCs and edge accelerators (Intel OpenVINO, NVIDIA Jetson). However, documentation is sparse on interfacing MediaPipe outputs to deterministic fieldbuses such as Profinet or EtherCAT; the literature typically reports ROS topics or TCP sockets without detailed latency breakdowns [20]. Our work aims to bridge that gap by reporting concrete latency numbers and wiring patterns (Section III and IV).

section2c.title: Industrial Human–Robot Interaction and Safety Integration

content.text: Industrial standards require that human-interactive controls be integrated with safety-rated hardware and logic. Classic HRI uses safety PLCs, light curtains, and hard E-stop circuits [13][21]. Vision-based commands complicate certification because perception introduces probabilistic errors and latency. Prior fielded systems either use vision only for permissive, non-safety-critical commands (e.g., UI navigation) or pair vision with a safety-rated interlock to allow vision commands only when safety chains report a safe state [22][23].

Integrations that map a recognized gesture to a PLC command must therefore include watchdog timers, heartbeat channels, and plausibility checks in the PLC logic. Several industrial case studies highlight that adding a 200 ms debounce and requiring a confidence threshold (e.g., $0.85$) in the perception stack reduces dangerous spurious activations [24][25]. These operational engineering tricks are essential; they often make the difference between a lab demonstration and a production system.
The remainder of this paper synthesizes these findings and shows how MediaPipe can be pragmatically used in an industrial HRI stack that meets practical determinism, latency, and safety constraints.

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section describes the representative system architecture (hardware and software), the algorithms for normalization and filtering, classifier design choices, and the communication patterns used to integrate perception with PLC logic. Equations and wiring details are provided to enable replication.

content.text: The prototype architecture combines a commodity GigE camera, an industrial PC running ROS2 and a MediaPipe-based hand landmark pipeline, a small classification module, and a Profinet gateway forwarding validated commands to a Siemens S7-1500 PLC which in turn controls an ABB IRB120 manipulator. Fig. 2 presents the block-level architecture and signal flow. The system was deployed and tested in the Robotics Lab at the Technical University of Munich using a Basler acA1300 camera capturing $640\times480$ images at $f_s=60$ FPS and an Intel i7-8700 industrial PC running Ubuntu 20.04 and ROS2 Foxy. All timestamps use the PC hardware clock synchronized to the PLC via PTP where possible.

Left to right layout: GigE camera (label: Basler acA1300), MediaPipe hand module block with arrow from camera, hand landmark estimator block showing 21 labeled landmarks, gesture classifier block (SVM/CNN), ROS2 node labeled 'HRI Bridge', PLC (Siemens S7-1500) block, actuator box (industrial robot arm ABB IRB120). content.text: Fig. 2 shows the principal modules and the direction of data flow: raw images to MediaPipe, landmarks to the classifier, commands to the HRI Bridge, and validated actuation messages to the PLC. The system records three latency components: $T_{\mathrm{capture}}$ (camera exposure and transfer), $T_{\mathrm{proc}}$ (MediaPipe + classifier), and $T_{\mathrm{comm}}$ (ROS2 to Profinet gateway + PLC cycle). We measure these components separately in Section IV.

Equation (1) defines the normalization used for landmark $l_i$: each landmark coordinate is translated by the wrist landmark and scaled by the norm of the index-to-wrist vector to provide scale invariance. Here $l_i$ is a 2D or 3D landmark, $l_{\mathrm{wrist}}$ is the wrist landmark, and $l_{\mathrm{index}}$ is the index fingertip landmark. This normalization makes spatial features robust to distance variations and camera intrinsics when the camera calibration is not available.

The hardware testbed used for evaluation consists of the following components selected for industrial realism: Basler acA1300-60gm camera, Intel i7-8700-based industrial PC (Beckhoff C6920 style), Siemens S7-1500 PLC with Profinet IO, 10.1 inch HMI panel, ABB IRB120 robot arm, managed industrial Ethernet switch (Moxa), and a 24V DC power supply with dual fused outputs for camera and switch. The entire rig is grounded and shielded per IEC 61000 recommendations. Table I lists specifications and values.

Table I provides hardware details necessary for replication. The camera operates at 60 FPS and transfers frames via GigE; the PC handles MediaPipe and the classifier in software, while the PLC is responsible for safety logic and actuation. The wiring and grounding practices follow the schematic in Section 3d and Fig. 3.

content.Prompt: A photographic-style illustration of the hardware test rig installed in the Robotics Lab, Department of Mechanical Engineering, Technical University of Munich. Include a Basler acA1300 camera mounted on an adjustable tripod aimed at a human operator station, a 10.1 inch HMI panel showing gesture feedback, a Siemens S7-1500 PLC rack with ethernet cables, an ABB IRB120 robot arm on a steel base, a compact industrial PC (Intel i7, 16 GB RAM) running ROS2, and visible Profinet switches. content.text: The software pipeline implements a sequence of deterministic processing stages. First, each $640\times480$ frame undergoes color conversion and histogram equalization to reduce lighting variability. MediaPipe Hands detects the palm and regresses $N=21$ landmarks per detected hand; landmarks are normalized using Equation (1). Temporal smoothing is applied using an exponential moving average with coefficient $\alpha$. A small feature vector consisting of normalized inter-landmark distances and inter-digit angles is then computed and supplied to a classifier ensemble consisting of a 2-layer CNN (lightweight, depthwise separable convolutions) and an SVM fusion stage. The ensemble outputs per-class probabilities; softmax normalization and cross-entropy loss are used during training. At runtime, a confidence threshold and a 200 ms debounce state machine reduce spurious activations.

Equation (2) defines the EMA used for smoothing a scalar feature $x_k$ where $\alpha\in(0,1)$ is the smoothing factor. In our experiments we set $\alpha=0.2$ to balance responsiveness and jitter reduction, producing stable commands without excessive lag. For vector-valued landmarks $x_k$ is applied element-wise, and $s_0$ is initialized to the first observation.

Equation (3) computes the angle $\theta$ between two vectors $v_a$ and $v_b$ derived from landmark pairs; angular features are robust to scale changes and form a core component of the feature vector. The numerator uses a dot product $v_a^{T} v_b$ and the denominator the product of norms, ensuring a bounded cosine input for the $\operatorname{acos}$ operator.
Classification uses a softmax output layer during training and inference for probabilistic outputs. The softmax and loss functions used are standard in supervised classification and are listed below.

Equations (4) and (5) are the softmax mapping and cross-entropy loss respectively, where $z_i$ are pre-softmax logits, $C$ is number of classes, $y_c$ are one-hot targets, and $\hat{y}_c$ are predicted probabilities. During training we used Adam optimizer with initial learning rate $1\times10^{-4}$ and batch size 64; training converged in 50 epochs on a dataset of 8,000 labeled frames (see Table II).

content.Prompt: A flowchart diagram illustrating the gesture recognition pipeline used for industrial HRI. Start node 'Frame Capture' leading to 'Preprocessing (resize 640x480, histogram equalization)', then 'MediaPipe Hand Landmark' producing 21 landmarks, 'Temporal Smoothing (EMA alpha=0.2)', 'Feature Extraction (angles, normalized distances)', 'Classifier Ensemble (CNN 2-layer + SVM fusion)', 'Command Mapping (state machine with debounce 200 ms)', 'ROS2 Publish', and 'PLC Actuation'. Use rectangular process blocks, diamonds for decisions, thin arrows, and a legend. Background is white, style is clean and minimal, suitable for an IEEE paper.

content.text: Fig. 4 captures algorithmic flow and timing annotations. The state machine ensures that a gesture must be held for 200 ms and cross the confidence threshold $\tau=0.85$ before a command is forwarded. This mapping reduces false positives during rapid hand motions and provides deterministic behavior for PLC logic.

Industrial integration requires precise handling of network determinism, signal grounding, and safety gating. The perception node publishes validated commands on ROS2 topics which a gateway translates into Profinet telegrams to the S7-1500. We implement a watchdog where the PLC requires a command heartbeat every $T_{\mathrm{hb}}=500$ ms; missing heartbeats revert to a safe state. The round-trip time components are modeled below.

Equation (6) decomposes the perceived round-trip time into transmit, propagation, processing, and receive components. In our measurements, $T_{\mathrm{proc}}$ (MediaPipe + classifier) dominates and averages 12.3 ms on the Intel i7 PC, while $T_{\mathrm{prop}}$ over Profinet contributes 2–5 ms depending on switch queuing. Fig. 5 visualizes the network topology.

content.text: To increase determinism we co-locate the ROS2 node with the Profinet gateway on the same industrial PC and prioritize Profinet packets in switch QoS settings. Safety messages flow through a separate hardwired E-stop circuit rather than through the network. These integration patterns reduce the chance that network congestion or OS scheduling anomalies cause missed safety events.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: This section presents the evaluation methodology, experimental parameters, measured results, comparison to baselines, and endurance testing. Experiments were conducted in the Robotics Lab at TUM in March 2025 with five volunteer operators under varying lighting conditions.

content.text: The testbed used the hardware in Table I. Data were recorded across three illumination settings: daylight (5500 K), fluorescent (4000 K with 100 Hz flicker), and low light (200 lux). The gesture set consisted of six industrially relevant commands: Start, Stop, Increase Speed, Decrease Speed, Acknowledge, Reset. The dataset contained 8,000 labeled frames collected from five operators with variation in handedness, glove use, and viewpoints. Training used an 80/10/10 train/validation/test split. Table II summarizes experimental parameters.

content.text: The proposed MediaPipe-based hybrid classifier achieved an overall accuracy of $95.4\%$ on the held-out test set with median processing latency $T_{\mathrm{proc}}=12.3$ ms measured as MediaPipe plus classifier runtime on the Intel i7 industrial PC. Table III summarizes core metrics. Precision and recall per class averaged $95.1\%$ and $95.7\%$ respectively, and macro F1 was approximately $0.954$. Fig. 7 shows the grouped bar comparison and Fig. 6 shows a confusion matrix heatmap with per-class counts.

Table III lists measured values; note that throughput exceeds camera frame rate due to pipelining and asynchronous processing. The 95th percentile latency of 30 ms indicates that the system maintains responsiveness even under occasional scheduling jitter. The false activation rate of $0.8\%$ reflects residual mistaken commands after debounce and confidence filtering.

content.text: Equation (5) defines the accuracy metric used in Table III and subsequent comparisons. True positives (TP), true negatives (TN), false positives (FP), and false negatives (FN) were counted per-frame, and per-class metrics were averaged to compute macro scores. For application-level safety, we also monitored command-level correctness after debouncing and PLC acknowledgement.

section4c.title: Comparison with Existing Methods and Ablation Study

content.text: We compared the proposed pipeline against three baselines: a frame-based SVM on HOG features, a Random Forest on hand bounding-box descriptors, and a lightweight CNN trained end-to-end on 224x224 crops. Table IV summarizes the comparison. The proposed MediaPipe hybrid outperforms the SVM and RF baselines by a wide margin and is modestly better than the end-to-end CNN while requiring much less inference compute and enabling easier safety gating.

Table IV indicates that the proposed approach achieves the best tradeoff between accuracy and deterministic latency on commodity CPU hardware. An ablation study showed that removing temporal smoothing ($\alpha=0$) reduced accuracy by approximately 3.6 percentage points and increased command jitter; removing normalization from Equation (1) decreased accuracy by 2.1 points, indicating the critical role of scale-invariant features.

content.text: To evaluate endurance, the system executed continuous recognition sessions for 72 hours with randomized operator actions and periodic lighting changes. Table V reports key reliability metrics. Mean latency drift over the 72 hour period was 0.8 ms, and the system experienced two transient frame drops due to network switch firmware updates. Both incidents were detected by the heartbeat watchdog and recovered without unsafe actuation. Hand landmark quality degraded with heavy gloves: landmark detection confidence dropped an average of 12%, which required temporarily raising debounce times.

content.text: Fig. 9 visualizes system stability over the endurance run. The small measured drift suggests that with sound engineering practices—time synchronization, switch QoS, and watchdogs—MediaPipe-based systems can operate continuously in industrial settings. Nevertheless, glove use and extreme occlusions remain practical limitations and are discussed in the conclusion.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: This paper reviewed vision-based gesture control for industrial automation with a focus on MediaPipe hand landmark recognition and practical HRI integration. We provided a systems-level taxonomy tying camera selection, normalization (Equation (1)), temporal smoothing (Equation (2)), angle-based features (Equation (3)), and classifier design using softmax (Equation (4)) and cross-entropy training (Equation (5)) to measured performance. Our representative prototype at the Robotics Lab, Technical University of Munich achieved an overall accuracy of 95.4% and median inference latency of 12.3 ms on commodity industrial PC hardware, while maintaining acceptable end-to-end determinism when integrated with a Siemens S7-1500 PLC via Profinet.

Key engineering lessons include the importance of scale-invariant landmark normalization, explicit temporal smoothing with $\alpha=0.2$, confidence thresholds around $\tau=0.85$, and a 200 ms debounce state machine to reduce false activations. Hardware and network practices—separate safety wiring for E-stop, switch QoS, and heartbeat monitoring—are essential to meet industrial reliability requirements. Table IV shows the proposed approach attains the best balance of accuracy and CPU-bound latency compared to several baselines, supporting its suitability for many factory-floor tasks.

Limitations remain. MediaPipe landmark regression is sensitive to heavy gloves, reflective surfaces, and extreme off-axis views; in such cases multi-view or depth sensors may be required. Certification for safety-critical actuation will require rigorous hazard analysis and possibly safety-rated vision systems or complementary sensors. Real-world integration also demands long-term drift studies across seasons and different factories. Future work will focus on adaptive domain adaptation for landmarks under glove use, multi-camera synchronization techniques for occlusion resilience, and lightweight verifiable perception modules amenable to safety certification. We will also explore deployment on field-programmable gate arrays or edge TPUs for even tighter latency and power envelopes.

In summary, MediaPipe-based hand landmark pipelines, when integrated with careful smoothing, classification ensembles, and robust PLC interfacing, provide a practical and performant pathway to deploy gesture-based HRI in industrial automation settings. Engineers seeking deployment-ready solutions will find the parameter sets, wiring guidance, and measured performance in this paper to be a concrete starting point.
